articles.title: UI DESIGN SYSTEM & MARKDOWN SYNTAX DEMO
articles.description: Complete showcase of all typography, lists, code blocks, tables, and blockquotes supported by the markdown parser.
articles.subtitle: A reference specification demonstrating headers, list markers, code copy actions, and responsive tables.
articles.content:
# 1. Main Section Heading (H1)

This is a standard text paragraph (`p`) illustrating text rhythm and line spacing. It demonstrates inline elements like **bold emphasis**, *italicized terms*, and an external link to [Next.js Documentation](https://nextjs.org).

---

## 2. Subsystem Heading with Hash Decorator (H2)

Headers of level two automatically prepend a green hash tag indicator.

### 3. Nested Feature Header (H3)

Below is an unordered bullet list demonstrating custom `>>` list item decorators:

* **State Determinism**: Every interaction yields a predictable render output.
* **Stream Processing**: Data pipelines handle real-time event updates without UI blocking.
* **Zero Overhead**: Minimal layout shifts and targeted component updates.

## 4. Numbered Execution Pipeline (OL / LI)

1. Initialize execution context and hydrate incoming parameters.
2. Validate incoming request schema using strict type guards.
3. Commit validated payloads to the persistence storage layer.

---

## 5. Blockquote / System Note

> "Visible progress beats hidden effort every single time. Clear state boundaries keep client architectures simple and maintainable."

---

## 6. Inline Code and Code Block with Copy Action

To run the local development server, execute `npm run dev` inside your terminal.

```typescript
interface SystemSignal<T> {
  readonly id: string;
  readonly payload: T;
  readonly timestamp: number;
  status: 'IDLE' | 'PROCESSING' | 'RESOLVED';
}

export function dispatchSignal<T>(signal: SystemSignal<T>): void {
  console.log(`[SIGNAL_DISPATCH]: ${signal.id} - ${signal.status}`);
}
```

---

## 7. Comparative Data Matrix (TABLE)

| Architecture Layer | Core Duty | Runtime Target | Status |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **API Gateway** | Request parsing & security guards | Node.js Runtime | Active |
| **State Store** | Client cache & sync reconciliation | Web Browser | Active |
| **3D Engine** | Mesh configuration & rendering | WebGL / Canvas | Standby |

---

articles.title: MONOREPO INFRASTRUCTURE WITH PNPM WORKSPACES
articles.description: How to split Next.js frontend and Node.js backend into a pnpm monorepo with isolated Dockerfiles.
articles.subtitle: Isolated Dockerfiles, workspace filtering, and static export that stays compatible with GitHub Pages.
articles.content:
# Monorepo Infrastructure

This article describes the migration from a single Next.js app to a pnpm workspace monorepo.

## Why separate apps?

* Frontend stays a static export deployable to GitHub Pages.
* Backend runs independently on Node.js + json-server for fast mocking.
* Each app owns its Dockerfile, dependencies and AGENTS.md.

## What changed

* `apps/frontend` holds the Next.js app with `output: "export"`.
* `apps/backend` exposes `data/db.json` via json-server on port 4000.
* Root `pnpm-workspace.yaml` defines `packages: ["apps/*"]`.

> API base for the next stage: `/api/v1` — routes are designed by a dedicated agent.

articles.title: CONTRACT-FIRST API WITH T RPC AND SHARED ZOD SCHEMAS
articles.description: Why the API contract lives in code: shared zod schemas, envelope-less tRPC responses, and fail-fast data validation.
articles.subtitle: One source of truth for backend and frontend: schemas package, AppRouter types, and runtime validation at the data boundary.
articles.content:
# Contract-First API

A tRPC contract is not a document — it is code that both applications import.

## The layers

* `packages/schemas` — zod schemas and `z.infer` types. The single source of truth.
* `packages/api` — tRPC routers built on top of those schemas.
* Frontend imports only `type AppRouter` and gets end-to-end inference.

## Validation boundaries

1. Input validation — zod schemas on every procedure.
2. Data validation — `db.json` is parsed at startup, the server fails fast on invalid data.
3. Transport — queries use `GET`, mutations use `POST`, superjson for serialization.

> If the schema does not run anywhere, it is documentation, not a contract.

## Responses without envelopes

`articles.list` returns `Article[]` directly. tRPC already namespaces procedures by path, so `{ items: [...] }` wrappers only add noise on the client.

articles.title: STATIC EXPORT DEPLOYMENT WITH DOCKER AND DOKPLOY
articles.description: Shipping a Next.js static export as a static-web-server Docker image with build-args baked into the bundle.
articles.subtitle: Root-context Docker builds, NEXT_PUBLIC env baking, and runtime fallbacks that keep the site alive without a backend.
articles.content:
# Static Export Deployment

`output: "export"` turns the frontend into plain files. The question is how to serve and configure them.

## Docker build

1. Build from the monorepo root context so `packages/` are visible.
2. Compile shared packages first, then the frontend.
3. Copy `out/` and `public/` into a `static-web-server` image.

## Env vars are baked in

`NEXT_PUBLIC_*` values are inlined into the bundle at build time. Changing `NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL` means rebuilding the image, not restarting the container.

## Runtime resilience

Sections use react-query with a fallback to local mocks. The static export stays fully renderable even when the API is unreachable.

cases.title: VOYAGE ANALYTICS
cases.description: Real-time travel analytics dashboard with interactive maps and cohort-based reporting
cases.fullTitle: REAL-TIME TRAVEL ANALYTICS WITH INTERACTIVE MAPS AND COHORT REPORTING.
cases.subtitle: Travel operators needed live demand signals instead of weekly CSV exports and static pivot tables.
cases.problem: Travel operators made pricing and capacity decisions from weekly CSV exports. Demand signals arrived too late to act on, and every team built its own pivot tables in spreadsheets.
cases.solution: A single analytics dashboard with live event ingestion, interactive region-level maps, and saved cohort reports. Filters are URL-driven so any view can be shared as a link.
cases.results: Decision latency dropped from a weekly reporting cycle to minutes. Adoption spread to three departments without a single training session — the dashboard became the default entry point for demand review.

cases.title: KNOWLEDGE GRAPH
cases.description: Graph-based knowledge base that turns documents and notes into a queryable entity network
cases.fullTitle: TURNING UNSTRUCTURED DOCUMENTS INTO A QUERYABLE ENTITY NETWORK.
cases.subtitle: Notes, papers, and code docs converted into a persistent graph with community detection and path search.
cases.problem: Personal research scattered across documents, notes, and browser tabs cannot be queried. Connections between sources exist but stay invisible without manual cross-referencing.
cases.solution: An ingestion pipeline converts arbitrary inputs into typed entities and relations stored in a graph database. Community detection clusters the graph, and a path-search API answers 'how are these two concepts related' queries.
cases.results: The graph persisted through multiple pipeline rewrites without data loss. Retrieval by entity relation replaced keyword search as the primary way to explore the knowledge base.
